subsections.title: Anthropic API vs. AWS Bedrock

blocks.title: They aren't the same
blocks.content: Calling Claude directly against the Anthropic API (api.anthropic.com) and calling Claude through AWS Bedrock are two different integrations. Bedrock is the AWS service that exposes several foundation models (including Claude) under an AWS-native interface and billing, with authentication via AWS credentials (IAM) instead of an Anthropic API key.

subsections.title: The flow of a chat app

blocks.content: In a typical chat app, the user sees a simple interface — they type a message and get a response — but behind it there's a multi-step flow between the browser, your server, and AWS Bedrock.

steps.title: The server calls AWS Bedrock
steps.description: Using the Bedrock client to make the request

steps.title: The request includes the message and the model ID
steps.description: For example, the ID corresponding to Claude Haiku or Claude Sonnet on Bedrock

steps.title: Bedrock returns an assistant message
steps.description: With the response generated by the model

steps.title: The server forwards the response to the browser
steps.description: And the user sees it in the chat interface

blocks.title: Your server is the intermediary
blocks.content: The user's browser never talks directly to AWS Bedrock. Your backend server is the one holding the AWS credentials and making the request to the model — the same intermediation pattern used with the direct Anthropic API or with Vertex AI, to avoid exposing credentials on the client.

articles.title: Your First Request to AWS Bedrock

subsections.title: The three components of a request

blocks.content: Making a first request to Bedrock requires three components: a Bedrock Runtime client to connect to the service, a Model ID specifying which model you want to run, and a User Message with the text you're sending to the model.

subsections.title: Configuring the Bedrock client

blocks.content: AWS's Python SDK (boto3) is what's used to connect to Bedrock — not the Anthropic SDK. A client is created for the `bedrock-runtime` service, specifying the AWS region:

blocks.code:
import boto3

client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-west-2")

subsections.title: Model IDs and regional availability

blocks.title: Not every model is in every region
blocks.content: If you try to invoke a model that doesn't exist in the region configured on the client, the request fails with a cryptic 'model does not exist' type error. For example, if Claude Sonnet is available in us-west-2 but the client points to us-east-1, the request will fail.

subsections.title: Inference profiles: the solution to the regional problem

blocks.content: An inference profile solves the regional availability problem by automatically routing the request to a region where the chosen model is actually available. Instead of manually keeping track of which model is in which region, the inference profile already knows the model is hosted in several regions (for example us-west-2 and us-east-2) and AWS picks the right one for you, even if the client connected from a different region.

AWS calls this **cross-Region inference (CRIS)**. An inference profile defines a model and the set of (destination) regions Bedrock can route the request to. The ID follows a format with a geographic prefix + the model ID, for example:

blocks.code:
us.anthropic.claude-3-haiku-20240307-v1:0
eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0

blocks.title: Where to find the inference profile ID
blocks.content: In the AWS Bedrock console, the inference profile ID isn't in the main model catalog — you have to look for it under the 'Cross-region inference' section, or on each model's detail page, 'Regional availability' table → 'Inference profile IDs'. That's the ID used as `modelId` in the request, not the general catalog ID.

blocks.title: Geographic vs. Global cross-Region inference

items.title: Geographic (us., eu., apac.)
rows: Routes only within the prefix's geography (US, EU, APAC, etc.)
Designed for data residency / regional compliance requirements

items.title: Global (global.)
rows: Routes to any commercial AWS region worldwide
Designed to optimize cost when there's no data residency restriction
Currently only available for Claude Sonnet 4

blocks.title: Details worth knowing
blocks.content: There's no extra cost for the routing itself — pricing is calculated based on the region you invoke the inference profile from, not the actual destination region. Cross-Region inference can route to regions that aren't manually enabled in your AWS account (no need to opt in to each one). All cross-region traffic travels over AWS's internal network, encrypted, without going over the public internet. CloudTrail logs these requests in the origin region, with the `additionalEventData.inferenceRegion` field indicating where it was actually processed.

subsections.title: Structure of a user message

blocks.content: User messages in Bedrock have a structure that might seem overengineered at first, but it has a reason:
`content` is a list because a single message can combine different types of content — text, images, or other media types. That structure is what allows building multimodal requests.

subsections.title: Making the request with converse

blocks.code:
response = client.converse(
    modelId=model_id,
    messages=[user_message]
)

blocks.content: The method used to invoke the model is `converse`, not `messages.create` like in the Anthropic SDK. The response carries a fair amount of metadata; to get to the generated text you have to navigate the response structure:

blocks.code: response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]

subsections.title: User messages vs. assistant messages

blocks.content: There are two main message types: **user messages** (content you send to the model, `role: "user"`) and **assistant messages** (content the model generated, `role: "assistant"`). Both share the same `role` + `content` list structure.

blocks.title: Same shape, different role
blocks.content: The assistant message Bedrock returns follows exactly the same format as the user message you sent, only the `role` changes. That symmetry is what makes it easy to chain messages to build multi-turn conversations, reusing each model response as part of the next request's history.

subsections.title: Bedrock doesn't save messages

blocks.title: Every request is independent
blocks.content: Neither Bedrock nor Claude stores the messages you send or the responses you receive. Every call to the Converse API is completely stateless — if you send only the follow-up question 'And 3 more?' without the prior history, the model has no way to know what '3 more' refers to.

To maintain a conversation's context, your application has to keep the full list of messages and resend it entirely on every request — including both the user messages and the model responses you already received.

subsections.title: Helper functions to manage messages
Building the conversation step by step

blocks.code:
messages = []

add_user_message(messages, "What's 1+1?")
answer = chat(messages)
add_assistant_message(messages, answer)

add_user_message(messages, "And 3 more added to that?")
answer = chat(messages)
print(answer)
# "Starting with the result of 1+1 = 2, if we add 3 more to that, we get: 2 + 3 = 5"

blocks.content: Each model response is appended back to `messages` as an assistant message before the next question. It's that complete history — not just the last message — that gives Claude the context to understand that '3 more' is added to the previous result.

subsections.title: Roles have to strictly alternate

blocks.content: The message list must follow the pattern user → assistant → user → assistant. Never two user messages in a row, nor two assistant messages in a row.

blocks.title: It's not just a convention, it's an API validation
blocks.content: If you break the alternation — for example, adding two user messages in a row without an assistant response in between — the Converse API rejects the request with an explicit `ValidationException` ('roles must alternate between "user" and "assistant"'). If you need to send additional content with the same role, you have to combine it into a single message before sending it, not add it as a separate message.

subsections.title: The Converse API's system parameter

blocks.title: Same concept as in the Anthropic API
blocks.content: Assigning Claude a role via a system prompt instead of listing rules in every user message is the same **role prompting** technique already explained in Claude API → Prompt Engineering → Role prompting: the role conditions vocabulary, level of detail, and criteria consistently, without having to anticipate every possible case in the user's message. What changes in Bedrock is just how it's passed to the request.

blocks.code:
system_prompt = """
You are an AWS cloud support specialist. Your job is to answer user queries related 
to cloud hosting services on AWS.
"""

response = client.converse(
    modelId=model_id,
    messages=messages,
    system=[{"text": system_prompt}]
)

blocks.content: Unlike the Anthropic SDK (where `system` is a string), in Bedrock's Converse API `system` is a **list** of `SystemContentBlock` — objects with a `text` key. In practice a single text block is almost always used, but the list structure is the same reason `content` is a list in messages: it leaves room for other block types, like `cachePoint` (prompt caching) or `guardContent` (content to be evaluated by a guardrail).

blocks.title: The system prompt text can't be an empty string
blocks.content: The `text` field of `SystemContentBlock` has a minimum of 1 character. Passing `system=[{"text": ""}]` is invalid — if there's no system prompt, you should omit the `system` parameter entirely instead of sending it empty.

subsections.title: chat() function with optional system prompt

blocks.content: The `if system` check is exactly what avoids the empty-string problem: if no system prompt is passed, the `system` key isn't even included in `params`, instead of sending it as an empty list or empty text.

subsections.title: Specification vs. role: a concrete example

blocks.content: For an AWS support assistant, the alternative to a system prompt would look something like this in every user message — fragile because you have to anticipate every case, and the user sees all the internal instructions mixed in with their question:

blocks.code:
add_user_message(messages, f"""
DO:
  - Mention how to host things on AWS
  - List some setup steps
  - Mention related AWS services

DONT:
  - Mention how to host services outside AWS
  - Answer questions not related to AWS

{users_question}
""")

blocks.content: The effect shows even on questions that are on-topic but generic. Without a system prompt, "How do I host a Postgres database?" gets a broad answer comparing several cloud providers and self-hosted options. With the AWS-specialist system prompt active, the same question produces an answer scoped only to AWS solutions — RDS, Aurora, EC2 deployments — without mentioning competitors, and with AWS-specific setup steps.

With the same system prompt, an off-topic question like "give me a bread recipe" doesn't get answered — Claude declines and stays in its role, with no need for an explicit rule for that particular case. That's the advantage over the rule-list approach: it covers both scoping related topics and rejecting unrelated ones, without having to anticipate every case.

blocks.title: The system prompt is fixed per conversation, not per turn
blocks.content: You can change the system prompt between one conversation and another, but not mid-conversation — it's applied once, before the model sees any user message, and stays fixed for that entire message thread.

subsections.title: inferenceConfig instead of a flat parameter

blocks.title: Same concept, different location in the request
blocks.content: temperature controls how deterministic or varied the model's output is — the same parameter already documented in Claude API → API Reference. What changes in Bedrock's Converse API is where it goes: it isn't a flat request field like in the Anthropic SDK, but nested inside `inferenceConfig`.
`inferenceConfig` is the same object where the rest of the Converse API's sampling parameters go — not just `temperature`, but also `maxTokens`, `topP`, and `stopSequences`.

subsections.title: The default depends on the model, not on Bedrock

blocks.content: If you omit `temperature`, the Converse API doesn't apply a fixed Bedrock-specific value — it uses the default of the model you're invoking. For current Claude models, that default is 1.0, same as in the direct Anthropic API.

blocks.title: On Bedrock, the mutual exclusion with top_p applies as of Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 — not as of Opus 4.7
blocks.content: The direct Anthropic API blocks sending a non-default value of temperature, top_p, or top_k with a 400 error as of Opus 4.7 (see Claude API → API Reference). On Bedrock the restriction is different: Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 only allow specifying temperature or top_p, not both at once, and this doesn't apply to earlier models. It's the same principle — adjusting a single sampling parameter at a time — but with a different trigger depending on the platform.

subsections.title: top_k doesn't live in inferenceConfig

blocks.content: Unlike `temperature`, `maxTokens`, `topP`, and `stopSequences`, `top_k` isn't a base parameter of the Converse API — `inferenceConfig` has no `topK` field. For models that do support it, like Claude, you have to pass it separately in `additionalModelRequestFields`.

subsections.title: stopSequences: cutting generation at a marker

blocks.content: As soon as Claude generates any of the strings passed in `stopSequences`, it immediately cuts off generation and returns only what was generated up to that point — the sequence that triggered the cut isn't included in the text. For example, asking it to count from 1 to 10 with `stop_sequences=["5"]` returns "1, 2, 3, 4, " without the "5". With several stop sequences at once, Claude cuts at whichever appears first.

blocks.title: To know which stop sequence triggered the cut, you have to request it explicitly
blocks.content: `response["stopReason"]` is `"stop_sequence"` when this is why it cut off, but the actual value of which sequence matched doesn't travel in the response by default. You have to declare it in `additionalModelResponseFieldPaths: ["/stop_sequence"]` when building the request, and it then shows up in `response["additionalModelResponseFields"]["stop_sequence"]`. Unlike the direct Anthropic API, where `stop_sequence` is a top-level field on every response, in Bedrock it's opt-in.

subsections.title: converse_stream returns a generator

blocks.title: The concept of streaming is already covered in Claude API → Practical Guides
blocks.content: Why use streaming (incremental response UX instead of waiting 10-30 seconds) is the same reason on any platform. What changes in Bedrock is the concrete shape of the method and the events.

blocks.code:
messages = []
add_user_message(messages, "Write a 1 sentence description of a fake database")
response = client.converse_stream(messages=messages, modelId=model_id)

for event in response["stream"]:
    print(event)

blocks.content: `converse_stream` (not `converse`) immediately returns a dict with a `stream` key, which is an event generator — each one a dict with a single key identifying the event type. To extract just the text, you filter by `contentBlockDelta` and navigate down to `delta.text`:

subsections.title: The full event set goes beyond contentBlockDelta

rows: Starts a new content block — text, tool_use, or another type.
Incremental fragment of the current content block. The one most used to show live text.
The message finished. Carries the final `stopReason`.
Closes the stream with `usage` (tokens) and latency metrics.

blocks.title: There's no event equivalent to message_delta
blocks.content: In the direct Anthropic API (see Claude API → API Reference), `message_delta` carries the `stop_reason` and the `usage` count together, before `message_stop`. In Bedrock that information is split differently: `stopReason` travels inside `messageStop`, and `usage` along with latency only arrive in the `metadata` event at the end of the stream — there's no single event that combines both.

subsections.title: Errors also arrive as stream events

blocks.title: ConverseStream can end in an exception within the stream, not just a prior HTTP error
blocks.content: If something fails during generation — throttling, an internal model error, a validation issue — the event can arrive as an exception key within the same stream (`throttlingException`, `validationException`, `modelStreamErrorException`, `internalServerException`, `serviceUnavailableException`), not as an error HTTP status before events start arriving. The code consuming the stream has to check for these keys in addition to `contentBlockDelta`, or the error goes unnoticed.

subsections.title: Streaming doesn't change the cost

blocks.title: Billed by tokens generated, not by how they're delivered
blocks.content: Using `converse_stream` instead of `converse` doesn't change the price: the model generates the same tokens, streaming only changes the transport (they arrive in chunks via events instead of all together at the end). The `usage` count that arrives in the `metadata` event reflects the same calculation you'd get without streaming. If your application closes the connection as soon as it has what it needs, it can even come out cheaper — you're only billed for the tokens generated up to that point, not for a full response that was never finished generating.

subsections.title: Message helpers need to accept multi-part content

blocks.content: Multi-turn conversations → Helper functions for handling messages defines `add_user_message`/`add_assistant_message` assuming `content` is always a string. That stops being enough as soon as tool use enters the picture: an assistant message with tool use carries text and `toolUse` blocks mixed in the same `content` list, and a user message with a tool result carries `toolResult` blocks, not text. The helpers need to accept both shapes.

blocks.title: Extracting text with content[0]["text"] is fragile
blocks.content: When Claude requests a tool, `content` carries several parts — typically text explaining the intent followed by one or more `toolUse` blocks. Reading only `content[0]["text"]` assumes the first part is always text and that there's exactly one text part; if the order changes or the text is split across more than one block, it either raises a `KeyError` or silently drops content. It's more robust to walk every part and join the ones that have `text`: `"\n".join(p["text"] for p in parts if "text" in p)`.

subsections.title: toolConfig: the equivalent of tools in the Converse API

blocks.title: Same concept, different shape
blocks.content: Declaring tools so the model can request their execution is the same tool use technique already documented in Claude API → Tool Use. What changes in Bedrock's Converse API is the parameter name (`toolConfig` instead of `tools`) and the nested shape of each tool's schema.
`toolConfig` accepts two keys: `tools` (required, the list of tools) and `toolChoice` (optional — if omitted, the default is already `{"auto": {}}`, the model decides freely).

subsections.title: toolSpec: the schema nested under inputSchema.json

blocks.content: Each entry in `tools` wraps the schema in a `toolSpec` key with `name`, `description`, and `inputSchema`. The difference from the Anthropic SDK (where `input_schema` is directly the JSON Schema) is that in Bedrock the actual JSON Schema sits one level deeper, under `inputSchema.json`.

blocks.title: The most common mistake: putting the JSON Schema directly in inputSchema
blocks.content: `inputSchema` is itself a Union object — its only documented member is `json`. Writing `"inputSchema": {"type": "object", ...}` instead of `"inputSchema": {"json": {"type": "object", ...}}` is the most frequent nesting mistake when porting a schema from the Anthropic SDK.

blocks.title: strict: structured output enforcement at the tool level
blocks.content: `ToolSpecification` also accepts an optional boolean `strict` field, to force that tool's output to strictly follow the schema. It wasn't present in earlier versions of the Converse API — if the goal is guaranteed structured output, confirm the chosen model supports it before relying on it.

subsections.title: toolChoice: auto, any, and the tool exception

rows: Default. The model freely decides whether to use a tool or respond with text.
The model must request some tool from the list — it can't respond with text alone.
Forces a specific tool. Only supported by Anthropic Claude 3 and Amazon Nova models per AWS documentation — don't assume it applies to every model on Bedrock.

blocks.title: tool isn't universal across Bedrock models
blocks.content: Unlike `auto` and `any`, forcing a specific tool with `{"tool": {"name": "..."}}` is a per-model capability, not a guarantee of the Converse API in general. Check the chosen model's availability before relying on this mode for structured output.

subsections.title: The loop: toolUse and toolResult blocks

rows: `content` always as a list of content blocks, e.g. `[{"text": "..."}]`

blocks.title: status is only read by some models
blocks.content: The `status` field of `toolResult` is documented as supported only by Amazon Nova and Anthropic Claude 3 and 4 — it isn't a generic Converse API property. With other models, communicating a tool failure depends entirely on the text inside `content`, not on this field.

The rest of the principle is identical to the Anthropic SDK: the model's full response (`result["parts"]`, including text and `toolUse` blocks) is re-added as-is as an `assistant` message, and all `toolResult` blocks from the same turn travel together inside a single `user` message.

blocks.title: The request that sends the toolResult also needs toolConfig
blocks.content: Just like with `tools` in the Anthropic SDK (see Claude API → Tool Use), passing `toolConfig` only on the first request and dropping it on the next one breaks the context: Bedrock needs the `toolSpec` entries available to interpret the `toolUse`/`toolResult` blocks already sitting in the `messages` history, not just to decide whether to request a new tool. Every call to `chat(messages, tools=[...])` in the conversation has to keep passing the same tools list, including the one that closes the loop with the result already folded in.

subsections.title: stopReason: it's not just 4 values

blocks.content: The field that decides whether to keep looping (`stopReason != "tool_use"`) has quite a few more possible values than usually get mentioned. Worth knowing the full set, not just the ones that show up in one particular example:

rows: The model finished its response naturally.
The model wants a tool to be executed.
The `maxTokens` limit was reached before finishing.
One of the strings passed in `stopSequences` appeared.
A configured guardrail blocked or modified the response.
The content was filtered by content policies.
The model generated output that couldn't be parsed correctly.
The model requested a tool with arguments that don't match the declared `inputSchema`.
The input exceeded the model's context window.

blocks.title: A loop that only checks != "tool_use" treats everything else as success
blocks.content: The `if stop_reason != "tool_use": break` pattern correctly separates "wants a tool" from "finished", but it lumps `end_turn` together with `max_tokens`, `content_filtered`, `guardrail_intervened`, and the rest under the same exit branch. For a production application it's worth distinguishing `end_turn` (a genuine success) from the other cases (a cut-off, blocked, or invalid response) instead of assuming any value other than `tool_use` means everything went fine.

subsections.title: The complete loop: run_conversation

blocks.code:
def run_conversation(messages):
    while True:
        result = chat(
            messages,
            tools=[
                get_current_datetime_schema,
                add_duration_to_datetime_schema,
                set_reminder_schema,
            ],
        )

        add_assistant_message(messages, result["parts"])
        print(result["text"])

        if result["stop_reason"] != "tool_use":
            break

        tool_result_parts = run_tools(result["parts"])
        add_user_message(messages, tool_result_parts)

    return messages

blocks.content: This is the same loop already documented conceptually in Claude API → Tool Use → The multi-turn loop, adapted to Bedrock's helper functions and `stopReason`: each pass calls `chat()`, re-adds the full response as an `assistant` message, and if the stop reason was `tool_use`, runs the tools and re-adds the result as a `user` message before calling Claude again.

subsections.title: Example: splitting a task into several tools due to model weaknesses

blocks.content: A reminder system ("remind me about my appointment, it's a week from Tuesday") can't be solved with a single `set_reminder(when: string)` tool that relies on the model computing the exact date on its own: Claude may know today's date, but not always the exact time, isn't reliable at compound date arithmetic (months with different lengths, leap years), and has no native way to set a reminder. The fix is to expose each step as its own tool.

items.title: get_current_datetime
items.description: No required parameters. Returns the formatted current date/time — the starting point Claude can't assume on its own.

items.title: add_duration_to_datetime
items.description: Takes a date, a duration, and a unit (days, weeks, months, years...). Does the actual arithmetic in Python instead of letting the model infer it in text.

items.title: set_reminder
items.description: Takes the content and an already-resolved timestamp — never a relative expression like 'next week'.

blocks.title: A third reason to split tools, distinct from Claude API → Tool Use
blocks.content: The tool granularity section already documents that splitting tools makes sense when inputs are structurally distinct. This case is a different, independent reason: isolating as its own tool a computation step the model can't reliably solve in text (date arithmetic, time zone conversion), even if it's conceptually 'one request' from the user's perspective.

subsections.title: batch_tool in pre-Claude 4 models: why declaring it isn't enough

blocks.content: Claude API → Tool Use already documents that the `batch_tool` pattern (a meta-tool that groups several invocations) became obsolete with Claude 4+, which parallelizes independent tool calls by default. That improved default isn't guaranteed on Bedrock if the model behind the inference profile predates Claude 4.

blocks.title: With Claude 3.7 Sonnet, the model called the three tools in separate turns
blocks.content: Running this example against `us.anthropic.claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219-v1:0` (Claude 3.7, a generation prior to Claude 4), the model resolved "remind me about my appointment, it's a week from Tuesday" with three sequential turns — get_current_datetime, then add_duration_to_datetime, then set_reminder — despite having `batch_tool` declared and available. It didn't even use it: declaring the tool doesn't force its use. To parallelize on a pre-Claude 4 model, you need an explicit system prompt instruction — exposing the batch_tool schema alone isn't enough.

If that reinforcement is still needed (for example, for a case with many independent operations, like "What is March 12th + 50 days? And + 100 days?"), the `batch_tool` schema is implemented just like any other Bedrock tool — wrapped in `toolSpec`, with the JSON Schema under `inputSchema.json`:
`arguments` is a string, not an object: each invocation arrives JSON-encoded, and `run_batch` decodes it before dispatching to `run_tool` — the same router that already handles every other tool:

blocks.title: batch_tool is the one branch that doesn't splat with **
blocks.content: Every other tool is called as `get_current_datetime(**tool_input)` — the dict gets unpacked because each key is a named parameter of the real function. `batch_tool` is different: `run_batch(tool_input)` receives the whole dict as-is, because it needs the `invocations` key as a structure, not as loose function arguments.

blocks.title: batch_tool saves round-trips with the model, it doesn't give you concurrency for free
blocks.content: These are two separate benefits, and only the first one is automatic. (1) Fewer round-trips: instead of Claude resolving N independent operations across N sequential turns (each one a round-trip to `converse()`), it packs them all into a single `batch_tool` invocation — that much you get just by declaring the tool. (2) Real concurrent execution: `run_batch` as shown above is a plain sequential `for` loop in Python, running each invocation one after another. If you also need true parallel execution, you have to add a `ThreadPoolExecutor` (or another concurrency mechanism) inside `run_batch` — the same pattern already used by the `ThreadPoolExecutor` in Claude API → Tool Use for Anthropic's native parallel tool_use case.

subsections.title: Structured output by forcing a tool

blocks.title: The same technique already documented in Claude API → Prefill and Alternatives
blocks.content: Forcing `tool_choice` onto a tool that doesn't represent a real action, but only the schema of the data to extract, is the technique already explained in Claude API → Prefill and Alternatives → Case 2: JSON with a specific shape. The only thing that changes in Bedrock is the syntax: instead of a flat `tool_choice`, you have to build the full `toolChoice` object.

With `toolChoice: {"tool": {"name": "..."}}`, Claude doesn't respond with text — it responds directly with a `toolUse` whose `input` is already the extracted JSON, shaped exactly like the declared `inputSchema`. There's no need to close the loop with a `toolResult`: the "tool" doesn't execute anything server-side, so it's enough to read `parts[0]["toolUse"]["input"]` and stop there.

The trick is `tool_choices.get(tool_choice, {"tool": {"name": tool_choice}})`: if `tool_choice` is `"auto"` or `"any"` it uses those modes, and any other string gets treated as the name of a specific tool to force. So `chat(messages, tools=[...], tool_choice="article_details")` automatically builds `{"tool": {"name": "article_details"}}` without having to write the full dict on every call.

blocks.title: Forcing a specific tool: the same model restriction already documented
blocks.content: toolChoice: auto, any, and the tool exception already warns that `{"tool": {"name": "..."}}` is only supported by Anthropic Claude 3 and Amazon Nova. For guaranteed structured extraction on other models, the native alternative is `outputConfig.textFormat` (see below).

subsections.title: to_json: a flexible tool instead of one fixed schema per use case

blocks.content: Declaring a tool with a strict `inputSchema` for every shape of data you need to extract doesn't always scale. The alternative is a single generic tool, with an `inputSchema` that accepts any property, describing the desired structure directly in the prompt text instead of in the schema.

blocks.title: additionalProperties: true moves where the guarantee lives
blocks.content: With `article_details_schema`, the `inputSchema` is the guarantee: Claude can't invent a field outside what's declared. With `to_json_schema`, `additionalProperties: true` validates nothing — the only source of truth for the expected shape is the prompt text (the `{...}` block with `str`/`List[str]`-style annotations). It's more flexible (one tool covers any extraction), but it loses the structural validation a strict `inputSchema` provides: Claude can skip `num_topics` or write `topics` as a string instead of a list, and no schema error catches it.

subsections.title: outputConfig.textFormat: the native mechanism, no tool involved

blocks.title: Bedrock's equivalent of output_config.format
blocks.content: Claude API → Prefill and Alternatives already documents that, on the direct Anthropic API side, `output_config.format` with `json_schema` replaced the trick of forcing a tool for guaranteed JSON: it's a real API-level guarantee, without the conceptual noise of a tool that doesn't do anything. Bedrock's Converse API has the same native mechanism, under a different name: `outputConfig.textFormat`.

blocks.title: schema is a string, not a nested dict — unlike toolSpec
blocks.content: In `toolSpec.inputSchema.json` the JSON Schema goes in as a nested object. In `jsonSchema.schema` it goes in as a **string** — you have to serialize it with `json.dumps()` before sending it, or the request fails. It's the most likely trap when migrating a schema already written for a tool over to `outputConfig.textFormat`.

blocks.title: Same decision criteria as on the Anthropic side
blocks.content: outputConfig.textFormat makes sense when the only goal is guaranteed JSON, without needing the model to reason about whether to use a tool. Forcing a tool with `toolChoice` is still preferable when extraction coexists with real tools in the same conversation, or when tool infrastructure (validation, logging) already exists and you'd rather reuse it than duplicate it.

subsections.title: The Text Editor Tool in Bedrock: it doesn't go through toolConfig

blocks.content: The Text Editor Tool (and its siblings `bash`, `computer`, and `memory`) are Anthropic-defined tools: the schema is already built into the model, so the declaration carries no `description` or `input_schema` — just an identifier. The app still has to implement the real execution (reading/writing files, running commands) and return the result; that part is already documented in Claude API → Tool Use → Tools provided by Anthropic for the direct API.

blocks.title: On Bedrock, these tools don't use the Converse API
blocks.content: AWS's documentation distinguishes two separate mechanisms under separate names: "Client-side tool use" (regular tools, available on both Converse and InvokeModel, with their own schema wrapped in `toolSpec`) and "Anthropic Claude tool use" (`computer_*`, `bash_*`, `text_editor_*`, `memory_*` — requires the Anthropic Messages API request format, via `InvokeModel`/`InvokeModelWithResponseStream` or the `anthropic` SDK's `AnthropicBedrock` client, not `client.converse()` with `toolConfig`). Adding the Text Editor Tool to the same `tools=[...]` list already used by `get_current_datetime_schema` and friends in a `converse()`-based `chat()` doesn't work — it's a different invocation mechanism, not just another tool in the same array.

blocks.code:
# Declaration: Anthropic Messages format, no toolSpec/inputSchema —
# type identifies the tool, name is the name exposed to the model
text_editor_tool = {
    "type": "text_editor_20250124",
    "name": "str_replace_based_edit_tool",
}

from anthropic import AnthropicBedrock

client = AnthropicBedrock()

response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="us.anthropic.claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219-v1:0",
    max_tokens=1024,
    anthropic_beta=["computer-use-2025-01-24"],
    tools=[text_editor_tool],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a one sentence description of ./main.py"}],
)
# response.content may carry a {"type": "tool_use", "id": ..., "name": "str_replace_based_edit_tool", "input": {...}} block —
# Anthropic format (snake_case, tool_use/tool_result), NOT Converse's toolUse/toolResult

blocks.title: The anthropic_beta header is mandatory, and the course never mentions it
blocks.content: Without the `anthropic_beta` header matching the declared tool version, the request fails — the correct `type`/`name` alone isn't enough. Each version of `computer`/`bash`/`text_editor` is tied to a specific beta value, per the table above.

blocks.title: This table changes — the course's note about "up-to-date IDs" still holds
blocks.content: The original course material correctly points out that it's worth checking AWS's documentation for current IDs instead of trusting a fixed value: as of this writing, the direct Anthropic API already offers `text_editor_20250728` (with `max_characters` support, see Claude API → Tool Use), but Bedrock's Anthropic-defined tools catalog doesn't list that version yet — it stops at `text_editor_20250124` as the newest one available there. Bedrock doesn't necessarily keep pace with the direct API's update cadence.

subsections.title: invoke_model with a Titan model_id, not a separate endpoint

blocks.content: The Claude API doesn't expose its own embeddings endpoint (see Claude API → RAG and Agentic Search → Quality Retrieval → Embeddings and Vector Search, where that step is solved with an external provider like Voyage AI). On Bedrock this isn't necessary: Amazon Titan's embedding models go through the same `invoke_model` used by any other Bedrock model — there's no separate API, just a different `model_id` pointing at Titan instead of Claude.

blocks.code:
import json

# client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", ...) already defined

def generate_embedding(
    text,
    embedding_model_id="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0",
    dimensions=1024,
    normalize=True,
):
    request_body = {
        "inputText": text,
        "dimensions": dimensions,
        "normalize": normalize,
    }
    response = client.invoke_model(
        modelId=embedding_model_id,
        body=json.dumps(request_body),
        accept="application/json",
        contentType="application/json",
    )
    response_body = json.loads(response.get("body").read())
    return response_body["embedding"]

rows: Only required field — the text to convert into a vector
1024 by default; also accepts 512 or 256 — no other values are valid
true by default — the same unit-magnitude normalization already documented in Claude API → RAG and Agentic Search → Embeddings and Vector Search
Optional list with "float", "binary", or both — defaults to ["float"]. response_body["embedding"] only appears if "float" is included; otherwise read response_body["embeddingsByType"]

blocks.title: Model access isn't enabled by default
blocks.content: Before the first call you need to enable access to Titan Embeddings in the Bedrock console (Model access) — like any third-party foundation model on Bedrock, it isn't available out of the box on a new account. If `amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0` isn't enabled in the region/account, `amazon.titan-embed-text-v1` (Titan Embeddings G1) works as a fallback: it accepts a simpler request (only `inputText`, no `dimensions`/`normalize`/`embeddingTypes`) and always returns `embedding` directly in the response.

The rest of the pipeline — chunking the document, indexing the vectors, computing cosine similarity, retrieving by top-k — is exactly the same one already documented in Claude API → RAG and Agentic Search. The only thing that changes on Bedrock is this one step: where the vector comes from.

subsections.title: additionalModelRequestFields: the one escape hatch that doesn't follow Converse's camelCase

blocks.content: What Extended Thinking is, what it's for, and how to decide on a `budget_tokens` value is already documented in Claude API → Advanced Capabilities → Extended Thinking — that conceptual explanation doesn't change on Bedrock. What does change is how you turn it on and how you read the response, and in this case the pattern isn't the same camelCase renaming already seen throughout this article (`toolConfig`, `stopReason`, `inferenceConfig`).

blocks.title: additionalModelRequestFields doesn't translate anything — it passes Anthropic's native body through as-is
blocks.content: The container field itself is camelCase, like the rest of Converse. But its value skips the usual translation: it's an escape hatch that forwards Anthropic's native request body untouched, so `thinking` and `budget_tokens` stay in snake_case inside it — verified against AWS's official example (`additionalModelRequestFields={"thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 2000}}`, from the Converse-with-Claude-3.7-Sonnet-reasoning guide). It's the only place in the whole Converse API where the two conventions mix.

blocks.title: The response doesn't use thinking/redacted_thinking — it uses reasoningContent
blocks.content: Unlike the direct Anthropic API (`thinking` and `redacted_thinking` blocks, see Claude API → Advanced Capabilities → Extended Thinking → Redacted thinking), Bedrock's Converse API returns a union-type `reasoningContent` block, verified against the official reference: either `reasoningText` (`{"text": ..., "signature": ...}`, the readable reasoning) or `redactedContent` (base64 data, when the reasoning tripped Anthropic's safety filters). The concept is the same one already documented for the direct API — what changes is the field's name and nesting.

blocks.title: The signature gets forwarded the same way as on the direct API
blocks.content: Just like Claude API → Advanced Capabilities → Extended Thinking → Thinking with multi-turn tool use already documents, if you forward a reasoning block in a later turn you need to include `text` and `signature` unmodified — AWS's own reference spells this out in the definition of `reasoningText.signature`. The `budget_tokens` minimum is still 1024, and it must be smaller than `maxTokens` inside `inferenceConfig` — the same constraint that already applies on the direct API.

subsections.title: source.bytes instead of manual base64

blocks.content: How to process images conceptually and vision-specific prompting techniques (structured step-by-step counting, one-shot examples) are the same regardless of API surface, and don't change on Bedrock. The direct Anthropic API's own current limits are also higher than Bedrock's — see the numbers below. What actually changes on Bedrock is the shape of the content block, and in one concrete way it's simpler than the direct API.

blocks.title: No base64.encode needed — verified against AWS's reference
blocks.content: The direct Anthropic API requires sending the image already base64-encoded inside `source.data`. On Converse, `ImageSource.bytes` accepts the file's raw bytes directly — AWS's documentation states this explicitly: "if you use an AWS SDK, you don't need to encode the image bytes in base64," the SDK handles it underneath. `format` only accepts `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, or `webp` — the same four formats the direct API supports.

blocks.title: Bedrock hasn't kept pace with the direct API's newer limits
blocks.content: The direct Anthropic API now supports up to 100-600 images per request (depending on the model) and 10MB per image — noticeably more generous than Bedrock's numbers. Porting code written for the direct API without checking these figures is a typical source of `ValidationException` in production. Also watch the encoding: even though `ImageSource.bytes` doesn't force you to base64-encode it yourself, the SDK still does it underneath to transport it — that inflates the actual transmitted size by roughly 33%, so to stay under the 3.75MB post-encoding limit it's worth keeping the raw file under ~2.8MB.

`ImageSource` is a union type: the alternative to `bytes` is `s3Location`, which points at an object already uploaded to an S3 bucket instead of sending the bytes inline in the request — an option that doesn't exist on the direct Anthropic API, useful for large or reused images without paying the cost of re-transmitting them on every request.

subsections.title: The document block and the required name field

blocks.content: How Claude processes a PDF visually and textually at once, and the citations mechanism, are already documented in Claude API → Advanced Capabilities → Multimodal: Images and PDFs. Bedrock's Converse API repeats the same pattern already seen in Vision on Bedrock — a `document`-type block with `source.bytes` instead of manual base64, with the same size and count limits already listed in that table — but it adds a required field that `image` doesn't have, and it supports quite a few more formats than just PDF.

blocks.code:
with open("earth.pdf", "rb") as f:
    file_bytes = f.read()

add_user_message(
    messages,
    [
        {"document": {"format": "pdf", "name": "earth", "source": {"bytes": file_bytes}}},
        {"text": "Summarize this document in one sentence"},
    ],
)

blocks.title: name is required — and AWS itself warns it's a prompt-injection surface
blocks.content: Unlike the `image` block, which has no `name` field, `document` requires it (`Required: Yes`, verified against AWS's reference): 1 to 200 characters, alphanumeric characters only, whitespace (no more than one in a row), hyphens, parentheses, and square brackets. AWS's documentation adds a warning that doesn't appear on any other Converse field: the model might interpret the content of `name` as an instruction, so it's best kept neutral (`"earth"`, not a sentence). This is a different nuance from the direct API's `title` field (see Citations further up in that same section), which is optional and purely cosmetic for identifying the source in citations.

rows: The only format the direct Anthropic API also supports
Spreadsheets — no equivalent on the direct API
Word documents — no equivalent on the direct API
The direct API covers plain text via `source: {"type": "text", "media_type": "text/plain"}`, but doesn't declare html or md as a format of their own

blocks.title: Converse also has native citations for document
blocks.content: Just like the direct API (see Citations further up in that section), Converse supports verifiable citations over a document's content by adding `"citations": {"enabled": true}` inside the block — verified against `CitationsConfig` in AWS's reference: a single boolean field, the same minimal shape as `citations: {"enabled": True}` on Anthropic's side. Bedrock also exposes a field the direct API doesn't have under that name: `context`, a free-form string to give the model information about how to interpret the document when generating citations.

`source` is, just like for images, a union type — but with more members: besides `bytes` and `s3Location` (same meaning as in `ImageSource`), `DocumentSource` also accepts `text` (the content already as a string, no bytes or base64 needed) and `content` (an array of structured blocks). For the simplest case — a PDF read from disk, like in the example above — `bytes` is still the most direct option.

subsections.title: Reading citations back out of the response

blocks.content: Unlike the direct API, which adds a `citations` field inside each regular `text` block (see Citations in Claude API → Advanced Capabilities → Multimodal: Images and PDFs), Converse returns a distinct block type instead: `citationsContent`, verified as a member of the same `ContentBlock` union that `text`, `toolUse`, and `reasoningContent` also belong to. Inside `citationsContent`, `content` carries the generated text (an array of `CitationGeneratedContent`, each with a `text` field) and `citations` carries the array of references — two parallel arrays instead of citations embedded inside the text.

blocks.title: Is documentPage.start 0-indexed? AWS's reference doesn't say so in prose
blocks.content: The direct API explicitly documents `start_page_number`/`end_page_number` as 1-indexed. AWS's reference for `DocumentPageLocation.start`/`.end` doesn't say so in words, but it does declare `Valid Range: Minimum value of 0` for both fields — a hint, not a confirmation, that Converse might number pages starting at 0. Before assuming either convention in production code, it's worth printing an actual response with citations and checking it against the source PDF's real page number.

`location` is, again, a union type — with more members than a simple PDF needs: besides `documentPage` (the one this example uses), there are `documentChar` (character-position location, the equivalent of the direct API's `char_location`), `documentChunk`, `searchResultLocation`, and `web` — meant for RAG or search scenarios where the source isn't a document uploaded directly in the request.

subsections.title: cachePoint: a separate content block, not an added field

blocks.content: The conceptual mechanism — what prompt caching is, why there's a TTL, what counts as an exact cache hit — is already documented in Claude API → Advanced Capabilities → Prompt Caching, and doesn't change on Bedrock. What does change is how you mark the breakpoint: the direct API adds a `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` field to an existing content block; Bedrock's Converse API instead inserts a new content block, `cachePoint`, as its own item in the array — not a field inside another block.

blocks.title: The same tools → system → messages order already documented on the Anthropic side applies on Bedrock — with one extra rule
blocks.content: Just like Claude API → Advanced Capabilities → Prompt Caching → Order matters: tools → system → messages already documents, Converse chains the cache in that same order — verified against AWS's guide: modifying `tools` invalidates the `system` and `messages` cache. The difference is that on Bedrock the minimum token count is evaluated against the cumulative sum of all three sections combined, not section by section.

subsections.title: The token minimum isn't a fixed 1024 — it depends on the model

blocks.title: The course teaches a 1024-token minimum, but that's no longer universal
blocks.content: Verified against AWS's guide: 1024 tokens per cache checkpoint is still correct for several models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2, Claude Sonnet 4.6), but the newer Claude models available on Bedrock as of this writing — Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5 — require 4096 tokens per checkpoint. This table changes with every new release, so it's worth checking AWS's guide for the specific model in use instead of assuming 1024.
The maximum of 4 cache checkpoints per request for Claude models is the same limit already documented on the direct API side (see Cache rules → Up to 4 breakpoints) — that doesn't change on Bedrock.

subsections.title: Simplified cache management for Claude models — something the direct API doesn't have under this name

blocks.content: Bedrock offers, only for Claude models, a simplified cache management mode: instead of manually calculating where to place each of up to 4 breakpoints, a single `cachePoint` at the end of the static content is enough. Verified against AWS's guide: the system automatically checks back roughly 20 content blocks from that breakpoint, looking for the longest cacheable prefix possible, without the caller having to predict the optimal placement in advance.

blocks.title: The automatic check only looks back ~20 blocks
blocks.content: If the static content extends beyond those ~20 blocks, the automatic check won't reach it — in that case it's worth going back to manual breakpoints (up to 4) or reordering the prompt so the reused content falls within that range.

`cachePoint` can also go inside `system` — which on Bedrock is already a list of blocks (see System prompts on Bedrock further up) precisely to leave room for a block like this one alongside the text block.

subsections.title: Reading the result: cacheReadInputTokens and the total-token formula

blocks.code:
usage = response["usage"]
print(usage["cacheReadInputTokens"], usage["cacheWriteInputTokens"])
total_input = usage["inputTokens"] + usage["cacheReadInputTokens"] + usage["cacheWriteInputTokens"]

blocks.title: inputTokens isn't the total when caching is active
blocks.content: Verified against AWS's guide: with prompt caching enabled, `inputTokens` represents only the tokens that were neither read from nor written to cache. The real total input token count is `inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens` — summing only `inputTokens` to measure cost or volume undercounts the full request.

The response also includes `cacheDetails`, with the TTL actually used for the write — useful for confirming whether a breakpoint with `"ttl": "1h"` really got stored with that extended TTL instead of the 5-minute default.
